rv.q: The new regime at the National has delivered its first bona fide hit.
This handsomely cast and mounted show reminded me of the work the late, great Howard Davies used to present in the Olivier: and that is a high compliment indeed.

Now they want to eat nice meals and complain — and Gorky has them squarely in his sights. The opening scene, which has characters clattering on and off the wooden boards of Peter McKintosh’s pretty white dacha set, is a slightly tedious whirl. Gorky does a lot of setting up.
The actors must work hard to make us care – but they do, and in some cases sensationally so.

Though the sprawling production’s energy flags at times and we never spend quite long enough on any one character, this remains a melancholy, impressionistic portrait of an era – like our own – marked by vacuousness and poised on the brink of sudden upheaval.
So this is a generational production, really, and whatever its flaws are, they shouldn’t put you off seeing the sort of luxury revival that the NT was made for.
Guilty of the excesses it seeks to satirise, the production certainly won’t discomfort today’s middle classes.

Still, the best moments of Summerfolk shine out, strikingly modern.
Everyone will be talking about this for months.
This version of Summerfolk, directed with verve by Robert Hastie, is 40 minutes shorter than its last incarnation on the National’s stage, when Trevor Nunn directed it some 25 years ago.

That manifest wisdom gives her vicious denunciation of an entire class of intelligentsia at a nightmarish end of summer dinner party all the more force, director Robert Hastie’s slow build to that climax fully vindicated.
Whilst it is widely lauded as a frenetic ensemble piece, there are key characters who will always need to make an impression if the whole is to have been deemed successful.
Yet, despite the hazy glow of this new version by siblings Nina Raine and Moses Raine, it’s a message that lands with a heavy hand.
So as the characters ponder the purpose of their lives, the audience is left to wonder about the purpose of the play.

Served by the deadpan working classes as if they are fattening up their employers before slaughter, Gorky’s bourgeoisie are an irredeemably self-pitying bunch who complain about the shallowness of life yet do nothing to deepen it.

cn.t: Critics find this National Theatre revival of Gorky's rarely staged satire handsomely mounted with a stellar ensemble cast, though opinions split on whether the sprawling adaptation feels unfocused or brilliantly captures pre-revolutionary Russian ennui.
